title: Babel (Genesis 11:1–9)
hook: a tower to make a name for ourselves, and the scattering

segments.voice: Yesterday, covenant: a bow in the clouds and a promise to every creature. What small promise did you keep to a living thing? A new week starts. Day three hundred forty-four.

A new tower goes up downtown, and somebody's name goes on the top in steel letters, lit up at night. A few years later, someone else builds higher. Genesis tells its own tower story in nine verses. After the flood, the whole earth has one language and one way of speaking. People move and settle on a plain in the land of Sennaar. And someone has a new idea. Not stone. Bricks, baked hard in a fire, with tar for mortar. A new technology. And with it, a plan.
screen: `A NAME IN STEEL LETTERS.` → `ONE LANGUAGE, ONE PLAIN.` → `BAKED BRICKS AND A PLAN.`

segments.voice: First, the plan, in the Douay-Rheims. They say: come, let us make a city and a tower, the top of which may reach to heaven, "and let us make our name famous before we be scattered abroad into all lands." Notice what they want. Not God's name. Their own. And notice the fear underneath: before we be scattered. A tower to hold everyone in one place, under one name. Second, the irony. The tower is meant to reach heaven, but the text says God comes down to see it. However tall, it's so small that God has to come down to look. Third, the scattering. God confuses their language so they can't understand one another, and they stop building and spread across the earth: exactly what they were afraid of. The city is called Babel. In Hebrew it sounds like balal, to confuse or mix up. It's also the Hebrew name for Babylon. Fourth, how the Church reads it. Babel isn't only a punishment. The Catechism reads the spreading of the nations as part of God's plan after the flood, a world of many peoples. And some Christian readers, Church Fathers among them, read Pentecost as Babel turned inside out. At Babel, one language breaks into many and nobody understands. At Pentecost, the apostles speak, and people from many nations each hear them in their own language. The Church even offers the Babel story as a reading at the Vigil of Pentecost. Not one name over everyone. Many voices, understood.
screen: `LET US MAKE OUR NAME FAMOUS.` · `GOD COMES DOWN TO SEE IT.` · `BABEL, BALAL: CONFUSED.` · `PENTECOST, BABEL INSIDE OUT.` · then, large: `NOT OUR NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do something without needing credit. Settle, and breathe. Think through the next day. Where could you do a good thing that nobody will trace back to you? Refill the coffee no one refills. Fix a typo in a shared document. Leave a kind review without your name. Pay a small compliment about someone to a third person, and not to them. Choose one. Notice the small itch to be seen doing it, and let it go. If you pray, you can offer it for God's name, not yours. The bell holds the time.
Babel. The city of the tower, built to make a name. In Hebrew it sounds like the word for confusion, and it's the same name as Babylon.
Your line: not our name. Today, do your one uncredited good thing, and don't mention it to anyone, even later. Day three hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: The Tower of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9) is one of the readings offered at the Vigil Mass of Pentecost, where the Church sets it beside the gift of tongues in Acts 2.

fork.reveal: God comes down, confuses their speech, and they scatter across the earth, the very thing they built the tower to avoid.

original.note: Hebrew: Babel, the name for Babylon. Genesis plays it against balal, to confuse.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about why there are so many languages.
what it means: people build to make their own name great and hold themselves together, and end up scattered.
what a scholar hears: Babel and balal, a Hebrew pun on Babylon; Christians read Pentecost as its reversal.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 11:4 partially quoted from memory ('and let us make our name famous before we be scattered abroad into all lands'); confirm.
Babel/balal wordplay (11:9) and Babel as the Hebrew name of Babylon: standard. 'Stepped temple towers' refers to Mesopotamian ziggurats (e.g. Etemenanki); confirm the general phrasing.
CCC 56–57: after the flood, humanity's division into nations as part of the 'cosmic, social and religious' order under the covenant with Noah. Confirm the paraphrase.
Pentecost as Babel reversed: a common Christian reading (Fathers, e.g. Cyril of Jerusalem). Confirm 'Christians have long read'.
Genesis 11:1–9 is an option for the first reading at the Vigil of Pentecost (extended form); confirm.

Editor review (days 333-350): the hook no longer claims 'every big city' or calls Babel 'the first version' of the race; 'drift east' replaced (the Hebrew direction is disputed; the Douay-Rheims says they removed from the east) with the plain of Sennaar; cut the unsourced ziggurat claim; 'Christians have long read' softened.
